Description
PhD Student – Mammal Community Ecology
The Shared Planet Group led by Dr. Alex Jensen and based at Texas State University is recruiting a PhD student to start August 2027. This PhD student’s research will focus on mammal responses to resource pulses, with field work likely primarily occurring somewhat locally. There is funding available for 4.5 years.

The core of this PhD project will consist of collecting observational and experimental data on mammal responses to resource pulses in the field. Examples of locally important resource pulses include persimmons, prickly pear, and acorns. Several approaches will likely be used to study these interactions, including camera traps, selective exclusion, and scat surveys. The PhD student will also be expected to lead a paper (one of their chapters) that complements their field project but utilizes existing large-scale data or synthesizes existing research.

The PhD student will be expected to mentor undergraduate students, be a collaborative member of our research group, and participate in Biology Department activities. There are funds to attend one national conference and one regional conference per year. Alex encourages people from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences to apply but can only consider international applicants that are already living in the US. The PhD student will not have to pay tuition but will be expected to teach (TA) during 4 semesters.

Description
Environmental drivers and spatial prediction of waterfowl breeding abundance, distribution, and population dynamics in the Prairie Pothole Region

Opportunity: Ph.D. Graduate Research Assistantship 

Program: Department of Forestry and Environmental Conservation | Clemson University

Location: Georgetown, SC (James C. Kennedy Waterfowl and Wetlands Conservation Center) and/or Clemson, SC (Clemson’s main campus). The location is flexible and depends on the needs of the student and project. 

Start Date: Spring 2027 (January) 

Last Date to Apply: September 30 or open until filled

General Description: A Ph.D. graduate research assistantship is available through the James C. Kennedy Waterfowl and Wetlands Conservation Center, Clemson University, beginning January 2027 (flexible). This position will support a collaborative research project with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s Region 6 & 3 Habitat and Population Evaluation Team (HAPET) to evaluate, refine, and expand spatially explicit models of breeding duck pair abundance, distribution, and recruitment across the U.S. Prairie Pothole Region (USPPR), the Northern Great Plains, and beyond. 

Background: The USPPR supports 30–50% of North America’s breeding duck populations annually. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has collected long-term monitoring data of breeding duck abundance and remotely-sensed wetland habitat information through the Four-Square-Mile Breeding Waterfowl Survey (FSMS) for nearly 40 years. These data are used in spatially explicit models (i.e., decision-support tools) to prioritize where and what type of wetlands and grassland conservation efforts should occur within the USPPR. Amid ongoing efforts to modernize the FSMS and derived decision-support tools, HAPET scientists recently developed new models of breeding duck abundance and recruitment; however, these models must be rigorously evaluated, tested, and expanded to new geographies and across different species before they can be operationalized. Thus, this work has the potential to directly inform conservation and policy decisions for breeding waterfowl in the most important landscape in the Northern Hemisphere. Derived products will be used for conservation prioritization and outcome-based effects analyses by the National Wildlife Refuge System, the Prairie Pothole Joint Venture, state wildlife agencies, and other conservation partners, and will help guide ongoing redesign efforts of the FSMS.

Objectives: The student will work closely with HAPET scientists and other partners to develop reproducible workflows and spatially explicit population models for use in decision-support tools used for waterfowl conservation. Core objectives are to (1) evaluate, extend, and/or refine breeding waterfowl models and (2) quantify sensitivity to changes in survey design or sampling intensity. The student will have the freedom to develop additional objectives in collaboration with their advisor and HAPET staff (e.g., data integration, community models, dynamic detection probabilities). 

Fieldwork: While the research is primarily a modeling and remote-sensing based project, the student will join HAPET staff for 1–3 months in the USPPR (Bismarck, ND) to assist with FSMS surveys, aerial photography and habitat mapping, pre-season banding, and other fieldwork and related activities. Fieldwork will give the student firsthand knowledge of the survey data used in models and provide the unique opportunity to interact with HAPET staff and partners in the USPPR that use these models to support conservation prioritization, outcome analyses, and policy decisions.

Qualifications: Ideal candidates will hold an M.S. degree in wildlife ecology, natural resources management, computational biology, statistics, geospatial information science, or a related field. Preference will be given to applicants with a strong quantitative background (e.g., GIS, Google Earth Engine, R, JAGS) and knowledge and experience with migratory bird ecology and management. The position will involve extensive interaction and communication with federal agencies and NGOs, so strong interpersonal skills and the ability to communicate effectively in virtual and in person settings is essential.  

Expectations: (1) Willingness for summer fieldwork in the USPPR; (2) Publish results in peer-reviewed journals and present at scientific meetings; (3) A high standard of scientific and personal integrity.

Salary and Benefits: Student stipend will start at $32,500. A 3% cost-of-living increase can be negotiated annually, following satisfactory performance. Graduate tuition waiver and health benefits will be provided in accordance with Clemson University policies. Ample opportunities for professional development exist and can be strategically coordinated to align with the successful applicants career aspirations. 

Application Instructions: To be considered, please send as a single .pdf (1) a cover letter, (2) curriculum vitae or resume, (3) unofficial university transcripts, (4) and contact information for three references to Dr. Nick Masto (nmasto@clemson.edu). To ensure your application is received, paste “Breeding Waterfowl PhD Application” into the subject line of your email. Review of applications will begin immediately and continue until the position is filled.

Description
The Borderlands Research Institute (BRI) at Sul Ross State University (Dan Collins) in conjunction with Texas Tech University (Warren Conway) are seeking a motivated PhD student to conduct a doctoral project focused on movement ecology of cinnamon teal captured in southern Nevada on Pahranagat National Wildlife Refuge. This unique capture location lies in the heart of the interior Pacific Flyway and is a major bottleneck for birds moving through their annual cycle. This project will provide the opportunity to inform management decisions at multiple scales (i.e., local, regional, and national) by using (~ n = 100) GSM-GPS units that will address the objectives below. 

Objectives

1. Investigate Migration Strategies using the generated GPS data to estimate time spent on Pahranagat National Wildlife Refuge allowing managers to time management decisions and estimate duck-use days needed to support Cinnamon teal and other key migratory gamebird species as they migrate through the area. Additionally, linkages between  Pahranagat National Wildlife Refuge and associated breeding and wintering areas will inform conservation measures broadly. 

2. Perform Network Connectivity through a Random Forest modeling effort to investigate how important Pahranagat National Wildlife Refuge is to migratory game bird species such as Cinnamon teal as they are moving through managed wetland systems over the course of their annual cycle. 

Qualifications:

• M.S. in Wildlife Science, Natural Resources, Environmental Science, Ecology, or related field
• Experience or coursework in GIS/remote sensing and quantitative analysis preferred
• Demonstrated interest in movement ecology, wetland ecology, wetland dependent wildlife conservation, or resource selection
• Strong written and verbal communication skills
• Ability to work independently and collaboratively with agency partner


Additional Information
Sul Ross State University is in the initial stages of establishing a PhD program on campus. As they work towards that accreditation an agreement has been established with Texas Tech University for the student to spend time on campus at both Universities for course work. Dr. Collins and Conway will be Co-PIs. The student will also work closely with biologists from Pahranagat NWR (Rob Vinson) and Pacific Flyway state agency biologist (e.g., Nevada Division of Wildlife, Utah Division of Wildlife, Arizona Game and Fish Department). The opportunity to be exposed to multiple agencies, Flyways, and a unique academic setting offers the student the ability to gain access to more resources and individuals than many of their peers.

Description: I am recruiting one MS student to participate in an ongoing multi-year (2027-2029) project to assess population sizes, demographics, reproductive rates, growth rates, and survivorship of freshwater turtle populations in Mississippi. This will entail extensive trapping surveys, including mark-recapture, to capture, mark, and measure freshwater turtles, including at-risk and federally listed species. Together with an established doctoral student, the successful applicant will conduct repeated trapping and snorkel surveys at up to 12 established long-term monitoring sites in Mississippi for the alligator snapping turtle, Pascagoula map turtle, Pearl River map turtle, and other freshwater turtle species. We will also gather demographic information, including but not limited to survival and growth rates across size and sex classes, sex ratios, and clutch sizes. Data from these surveys will be used to estimate population density and assess population trends and extinction risk under different scenarios, using population viability analyses. Captured turtles will also be scanned for the presence of ingested fishhooks, so we can monitor the effects of these on individual health and survivorship. Mississippi boasts a high biodiversity of chelonians, including multiple species that are federally and state listed, or of conservation concern, and multiple single river endemic species. The information gained from this study will inform population viability analyses and other assessments for these freshwater turtle species, especially those of conservation concern. 
 Qualifications: Applicants must have a BS in ecology/environmental biology, zoology, wildlife biology, or other relevant areas. Academic record(s) must be competitive for admission to the University of Southern Mississippi graduate program in Biology. Prior experience with the safe operation of small motorboats and with trapping/handling of aquatic turtles is preferred but not required. Willingness and ability to work with a partner (for safety) is a must, as is the ability to conduct field work under potentially challenging field conditions, including high heat and humidity.

Description: The Beasley lab (http://www.beasleywildlifelab.srel.uga.edu) at the University of Georgia’s Savannah River Ecology Laboratory (http://www.srel.uga.edu) and Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources (http://www.warnell.uga.edu), in collaboration with the Ongava Research Centre (https://www.orc.eco/) is seeking a highly motivated M.S. or Ph.D. student to join a collaborative research team investigating herbivore and carnivore ecology and conservation within Sub-Saharan Africa. Through a combination of population surveys and movement studies, this research program is working to elucidate the underlying factors that drive African mammal numbers and their distribution, movement ecology, population dynamics, and to understand predator-prey interactions. The selected student will participate in ongoing research within this framework and be given latitude to develop their thesis questions within the study framework. The student will work in close collaboration with the Greater Etosha Carnivore Programme, other students, researchers, and agency personnel associated with this research. There will be opportunities to participate in both ungulate and carnivore captures along with various other research activities. While conducting field work, the student will be based at the Ongava Research Centre in Namibia. The start date for this position is summer 2027, with fieldwork beginning in May or June. 

Qualifications: Applicants at both the M.S. and Ph.D. level are encouraged to apply and will be considered. Minimum qualifications for this position include a bachelor’s degree in a related field at the M.S. level, and at the Ph.D. level a M.S. degree in wildlife ecology, ecology, or a related discipline. A demonstrated record of publication is required at the Ph.D. level. Prior experience conducting wildlife research is required and students must have excellent organizational, writing, and communication skills. Only applicants with strong backgrounds conducting field studies should consider applying. Preference will be given to students with experience conducting and managing camera surveys, capturing and handling mammals, and spatial/GIS/R experience. Prior experience working in African countries or other remote systems is highly preferred. Ability to drive 4x4 manual vehicles through rugged landscapes is required.

Application: To apply, please send the following in a single PDF document: 1) cover letter summarizing your qualifications for the position, 2) a CV, and 3) names and contact information for three references to Dr. Jim Beasley: beasley@srel.uga.edu. Applications will be reviewed starting on September 28th, and will continue until a suitable candidate is found. Description
The Lowman Lab in the School of Aquatic and Fishery Sciences (SAFS) at the University of Washington (UW) is recruiting a PhD student in watershed ecology and biogeochemistry to start in fall 2027. Applicants should be interested in conducting research on topics including, but not limited to, quantifying recovery and resilience of streams and rivers following large floods or other disturbances, the effects of wildfire on stream biogeochemistry, how compounding climate events impact aquatic primary productivity and nutrient cycling, how changing winter hydrology and precipitation shapes stream productivity (both primary and secondary), and how human modification of the landscape or flow regime alters stream ecosystem function and biodiversity.
 Graduate students in the Lowman Lab will be trained in foundational stream ecology methods and approaches, field ecology techniques, analytical chemistry protocols, data science and programming for ecological modeling, manuscript preparation, grant writing, and science communication. Students will also be encouraged to attend national and international conferences and workshops to present their findings, build their networks, and identify new career opportunities. At SAFS, the graduate student will join a dynamic and highly collaborative community of aquatic scientists and will have opportunities to join associated programs, such as the Quantitative Ecology and Resource Management Program. 
 Successful candidates will be: enthusiastic about watershed ecology and biogeochemistry; organized and detail-oriented with demonstrated experience managing research projects; and collegial and excited to collaborate as part of larger, multi-disciplinary research groups. There is also a possibility for the student to begin developing project ideas and gain experience as a field research technician in summer 2027.
 Interested applicants should submit a one-page cover letter (describing past experience, motivation to pursue a graduate degree, and reasons for applying to this position), a CV or resume, an unofficial transcript, and contact information for three professional references via e-mail to Dr. Heili Lowman (hlowman@uw.edu) by October 9. ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the Crop Production Systems Research Unit, U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), located in Stoneville, Mississippi.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: This research is a component of ARS National Programs 305 (Crop Production) and 304 (Crop Protection & Quarantine). Throughout the course of this project, you will learn about project management by contributing to research evaluating herbicide efficacy and screening for herbicide resistance in established and newly emerging problematic weed species in the Mississippi Delta region. You will also learn to identify key differences in physiology, growth characteristics, photosynthetic capacities, adaptability, competitiveness, and responses to stress and other fitness criteria of wild-type versus herbicide-resistant plant biotypes. You will contribute to studies examining how environmental conditions, cropping systems, and management practices influence weed emergence, competitiveness, and long-term persistence.

The project involves collecting, managing, and analyzing data related to weed control, herbicide performance, and whole-plant physiological processes of herbicide-resistant and susceptible populations under controlled environmental and field conditions. These insights are important for predicting the ecological success of resistant populations and developing more sustainable, integrated weed management strategies. This project will also involve close collaboration with USDA-ARS scientists specializing in plant physiology, molecular biology, genomics, and herbicide resistance to advance understanding of resistance mechanisms and support the development of novel weed management solutions for problematic weeds in Mississippi cropping systems. Through participation in this research project, you will gain experience operating specialized equipment such as spray chambers and LI-COR gas-exchange systems, as well as opportunities for managing field, growth-chamber, and greenhouse studies to investigate weed control in cropping systems.

Gain hands-on research experience in agronomy/weed science and herbicide resistance screening across multiple species;
Learn to operate specialized equipment such as an research track sprayer, leaf area meter, root scanner, and LI-COR photosynthesis systems;
Develop strong competencies in collecting, processing, and analyzing plant samples to characterize herbicide resistance mechanisms; and
Build robust data analysis skills and enhance scientific writing and publishing capabilities.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Experience with physiological measurement tools and spray chambers (e.g., LI-COR gas exchange systems, chlorophyll fluorometers, research track sprayers).

Description
The Lawson Lab in the New Mexico Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit at New Mexico State University (NMSU) invites applications for a PhD research assistantship beginning in January 2027. The successful applicant will be part of an exciting collaborative study between NMSU and the New Mexico Department of Wildlife to investigate spatial and population ecology of the Lesser Prairie-Chicken. The student will be advised by Dr. Abby Lawson (USGS/NMSU), and work closely with Dr. Aaron Young (NMSU) and Mr. Grant Beauprez (NMDOW).

Lesser Prairie-Chickens have experienced persistent population declines throughout their range and were recently proposed for listing under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Energy development (oil and gas, wind turbines) and woody shrub encroachment resulting in habitat loss are thought to be contributing factors to the ongoing declines. This project is part of a five-year study to evaluate Lesser Prairie-Chicken movement and demography in response to translocations, transmission line development, and mesquite removal. The student will have a fairly unique opportunity to compare before, during, and after the construction of a major transmission line that runs through the study area in Milnesand, New Mexico. Two years of data have been collected and the student is expected to lead the remaining three field seasons. 

The student will be expected to develop cutting-edge research questions related to movement and population ecology, and be eager to work with managers. Other potential research topics could include developing decision support tools to target mesquite removal, evaluating the effects of translocations, or question related to trophic or thermal ecology.

In addition to the research project, the student will be part of NMSU’s Avian Migration Program, that prepares students for careers in applied avian conservation and management in a rapidly changing world. Graduate students in the program will receive training through a series of workshops, and have the opportunity to mentor undergraduates on a small research project associated with the Lesser Prairie-Chicken study.

Salary and Benefits
This position includes 4 years of funding for a research assistantship (~$29K/year), full tuition scholarship, and health insurance reimbursement (up to $200/month). There is also travel funding available for presenting research at local and national conferences.

Qualifications:
Required: B.S. in wildlife, environmental sciences, or related field and possession of a valid U.S. driver’s license. The successful applicant must also meet the minimum requirements for admission to the NMSU Graduate School (3.0 GPA in last two years of undergrad), as well as GRE scores for applicants who received the undergraduate degree outside the U.S. Applicants should also have demonstrated excellent written and oral communication skills and/or quantitative skills, experience conducting field work, and an ability to work independently while following safety protocols. This position is based in Las Cruces, NM with field work in Milnesand, NM; I am not able to accommodate remote work.

 Strong preference will be given to applicants who have completed an M.S in wildlife, ecology, or a related field, as well as applicants with a strong spatial ecology background (e.g., analysis of telemetry data, remote sensing, experience with R and ArcGIS). Previous experience in one or more of the following areas is also desired: upland game bird ecology, Bayesian hierarchical models, working with private landowners, and experience with threatened or endangered species.

 To apply, please submit an application through our online portal (link below). Applicants will be asked to provide the following in a single PDF: (1) letter of interest that describes their qualifications and how this position fits into their career goals; (2) CV or resume that includes contact information for three references (including a direct supervisor); (3) writing sample such as a published manuscript or M.S. thesis; and (4) university transcripts (unofficial is fine). Apply by September 28th for full consideration,  though the position will remain open until a suitable candidate is found.

M.S. or Ph.D. Assistantship at U of Wyoming studying the importance of mesic habitats for ungulate conservation  
The Merkle Research Group is looking for a highly motivated, creative, and quantitative M.S. or Ph.D. student to lead a project studying how ungulates use and rely on mesic habitats, as well as studying how to prioritize mesic habitat restoration to benefit ungulate populations. 

The project is a collaboration between Working Lands for Wildlife, Wyoming Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, and University of Wyoming. The primary goal of the project is purposefully broad, and the student will have the opportunity to shape their specific research questions accordingly. The research will primarily rely on previously collected GPS collar and remote sensing data related to mesic areas (see https://www.mesic.app/), and the position will have a heavy emphasis on data analytics over field work.

Candidates must have a B.S. and preferably a M.S. degree (for starting as a Ph.D. student) in Ecology, Wildlife, Computing, or related field. Applicants with experience managing and analyzing large spatial datasets (including remote sensing and animal movement data) in program R, working independently and with a team on research projects, and publishing peer-reviewed research will be favored. Successful applicants will be expected to participate in a collaborative team environment, co-produce high-quality research, present their work at professional conferences, and publish results in a timely manner in peer-reviewed journals. 

The successful applicant will be admitted through the Program in Ecology and Evolution at University of Wyoming and be based in Laramie (USA). A graduate assistantship will be provided, which includes tuition and benefits, and a monthly stipend of $2,000/month (M.S.) or $2,418/month (Ph.D.). To apply, please email a SINGLE PDF file that includes 1) a detailed cover letter outlining, at a minimum, experience and interest in studying habitat conservation as it relates to ungulates and analyzing animal movement data, 2) a CV, 3) contact information for three references, and 4) unofficial transcripts to Dr. Jerod Merkle (jmerkle@uwyo.edu) and Dr. Julie Brockman (jbrockm1@uwyo.edu). Description
The School of Natural Resources and the Environment at West Virginia University is searching for a master’s student to join a research team monitoring Ruffed Grouse populations in response to different landscape contexts and disturbances, including varying levels of timber harvests, prescribed fire, and cut-back borders. The students will use Autonomous Recording Units (ARUs) and spring drumming counts to determine occupancy and abundance of Ruffed Grouse. The students will also be responsible for sampling mosquitoes for West Nile Virus. Finally, the student will identify through ArcGISPro geospatial and landscape variables affecting Ruffed Grouse distribution, and model scenarios predicting Ruffed Grouse responses to future conditions. 

This project will occur across West Virginia on private and public lands. Ruffed Grouse and bird species utilizing young forests have declined precipitously, and the goal of this project is to identify landscape scale management strategies to improve populations via occupancy or abundance. Additionally, West Nile Virus could be a contributing factor in Ruffed Grouse declines, and in West Virginia data are lacking about the distribution and prevalence of the virus or mosquitoes. The students will also have opportunities and flexibility to develop and design additional research projects if they are within the scope of the main project questions. Additional questions about landscape context, conservation planning, and applicability to other ecoregions are potential options. 

The project will occur on multiple state wildlife management areas, state forests, and on Weyerhaeuser property. There will be significant traveling and potential for camping or living in rustic state field houses. The students should also have experience driving on gravel or dirt roads and with 4x4 vehicles. The data collection will begin in April and continue into August. Students should expect to be flexible with scheduling and work together to coordinate data collection schedules. Results should inform landscape level planning and management strategies for Ruffed Grouse and other young forest species. The research is funded through the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources, Ruffed Grouse Society, and National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. 

The student will be working towards a master’s in Wildlife and Fisheries Resources at West Virginia University. STARTING DATE: January 2027. Description
A Master of Science (M.S.) position is available at Auburn University. The incoming student will be a Graduate Research Assistant in Dr. Tim Bruce’s Fish Health Lab within the School of Fisheries, Aquaculture and Aquatic Sciences (SFAAS). Research in the Bruce lab focuses on host-pathogen interactions in cultured fish species, nutritional aspects of fish health, and fish vaccines/therapeutants.
 Responsibilities and tasks 
This M.S. project will involve experimental laboratory studies (~80%) and in vivo trial work with warmwater fish species (~20%). Specifically, this M.S. thesis research will examine microbial interactions using molecular techniques. The bacterial species involved in this project are relevant to U.S. aquaculture (catfish, largemouth bass, and tilapia), and the project will involve genomic and proteomic analyses. Overall, the student will be expected to conduct an independent research project, followed by the writing and defense of a detailed thesis.  

Qualifications 
The Bruce Fish Health Lab team is looking for a motivated candidate who has:

•   Bachelor’s degree in Microbiology/Biological Sciences 
•   Detailed knowledge of microbiology and/or fish health/immunology 
•   Proven ability to carry out goal-oriented work and fluent with data management systems and programming software 
•   Lab competencies in microbiology (e.g., culture, identification, sequencing, microbial-based assays)  
•   Molecular biology skills (e.g., SDS-PAGE/Western blot, gene expression [qPCR], proteomics) are also required. 
•   Assistance with fish husbandry and conducting aquaculture trials is also required 
•   Ability to work independently and in a team laboratory setting  
•   A driver’s license is required with reliable transportation 

Approval and Enrollment 
This M.S. graduate appointment is subject to academic approval, and the candidate will be enrolled in the M.S. program within the School of Fisheries, Aquaculture and Aquatic Sciences (SFAAS). For information about our program please see:  http://sfaas.auburn.edu/programs-of-study/graduatestudies/
 Salary and appointment terms 
This project will be carried out at the E.W. Shell Fisheries Center, which is situated in Auburn, Alabama (http://sfaas.auburn.edu/e-w-shell-fisheriescenter/). The student will begin coursework and research in Spring 2027.

 Please note that documents not sent within this format will not be reviewed.

Environmental Stewardship: plant native species, maintain wildlife gardens and landscapes
Property Stewardship & Groundskeeping: learn property management and facility maintenance of historic and new structures, routine general maintenance including lawn mowing and weed whacking
Community Outreach: assist with volunteer events, presentations, and educational activities that engage the public in conservation

Professional training in restoration and conservation

USDA Forest Service Office/Lab and Location: A fellowship opportunity is available with the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Forest Service (FS) within the Pacific Southwest Research Station (PSWRS) located in Hilo, Hawaii.

At the heart of the USDA Forest Service's mission is their purpose. Everything they do is intended to help sustain forests and grasslands for present and future generations. Why? Because their stewardship work supports nature in sustaining life. This is the purpose that drives the agency’s mission and motivates their work across the agency. It’s been there from the agency’s very beginning, and it still drives them. To advance the mission and serve their purpose, the USDA Forest Service balances the short and long-term needs of people and nature by: working in collaboration with communities and our partners; providing access to resources and experiences that promote economic, ecological, and social vitality; connecting people to the land and one another; and delivering world-class science, technology and land management.

The Forest Service’s Pacific Southwest Research Station serves the states of California and Hawaii and U.S. affiliated Pacific Islands. PSW’s program at the Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry performs a broad variety of research to benefit the land and people of Hawaii and Pacific Islands, including development of biological control as a tool for managing invasive species.

Research Project: Invasive species in Hawaii have devastating impacts on island forest and rangeland ecosystems and the lives and livelihoods of citizens. Ongoing efforts using mechanical and chemical control provide short term solutions for incipient infestations and small areas that can be intensively managed, but invasions by certain pests and weeds are so widespread that long term management will depend on biocontrol using host-specific natural enemies. Our research program identifies and evaluates biocontrol agents to measure their effectiveness and suitability for release in Hawaii for long term management of pests and weeds such as twolined spittlebug, fountain grass, albizia, miconia, clidemia, and strawberry guava. You will participate with Forest Service entomologists and ecologists in methods used to quantify the specificity and impacts of biocontrol agents for high priority pests and weeds. Mentoring by Forest Service scientists will ensure that you acquire skills to carry out a variety of activities important for evaluating and managing Hawaii’s forest ecosystems, including experimental design, plot establishment and monitoring, assessing plant health, and identifying insects and their damage.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), San Joaquin Valley Agricultural Sciences Center, in Parlier, California.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

The San Joaquin Valley Agricultural Sciences Center conducts research to support the sustainability, quality, and productivity of specialty crops industries across California’s Central Valley. The Commodity Protection and Quality Research Unit focuses on improving postharvest quality and reducing losses of horticultural specialty crops caused by fungal pathogens, physiological disorders, and the control of quarantine insect pests that threaten market access and export opportunities.

Research Project: We are seeking a highly motivated postdoctoral fellow to be a part of research focused on postharvest disease management and quality of fresh fruits. The fellowship has two primary learning experiences. You will examine the susceptibility of table grape breeding lines to gray mold caused by Botrytis cinerea, including developing and conducting scalable, high-throughput phenotyping methods to assess susceptibility and evaluate established or newly developed screening approaches. This also includes developing and evaluating preharvest and postharvest treatments aimed at controlling postharvest diseases of fresh fruits. This offers opportunities to contribute to high-value research that directly supports industry resilience and helps strengthen postharvest disease control.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of the mentor, you will:

Learn to conduct research focused on postharvest disease management and quality in fresh fruits.
Gain experience evaluating the susceptibility of table grape breeding lines to gray mold caused by Botrytis cinerea.
Develop skills in designing and implementing scalable, high-throughput phenotyping methods to assess disease susceptibility.
Learn to evaluate and refine established and newly developed screening approaches for postharvest disease resistance.

Ducks Unlimited (DU) seeks a Private Lands Biologist (PLB) to support delivery of wetland and waterfowl habitat conservation projects on private lands on the Texas Coast. The successful candidate will lead delivery of DU’s private land programs on the Texas Coast – Texas Prairie Wetlands Project and Texas Coastal Wetlands Program. With guidance from senior DU team members, the PLB plays an essential role in ensuring projects are delivered timely, accurately, and in compliance with funding and partnership requirements. Other responsibilities include annual monitoring of a small portfolio of DU conservation easements.

The position will be based out of the DU Field Office in Richmond, Texas with approximately 50% time in the field and 50% time in the office. A work truck will be provided for position duties. Most travel will be day trips with some trips requiring overnight accommodation. Typical field activities consist of meeting with private landowners on-site to discuss potential or ongoing projects. Master’s degree with an emphasis in waterfowl and wetlands.

Description
Student Services Contractor: Fish Biologist (Acoustic Telemetry Research)

Fish Telemetry Research | Pacific Northwest

We are seeking a current student or recent graduate (within one year of graduation) to join our team as a service contractor supporting several fish telemetry research projects. This is a unique opportunity to combine hands-on fieldwork with rigorous quantitative research on high-profile fisheries and water management issues.

About the Role

You will conduct field research on juvenile salmon and endangered sucker species in large lakes, reservoirs, and estuaries in the Pacific Northwest. Your work will directly contribute to our understanding of fish habitat use, movement, spatial distribution, and survival of these species. 

This position offers a dynamic, seasonal balance:

Less than half the year: Take a lead role in demanding field operations, deploying and retrieving telemetry equipment and collecting data from boats in dynamic aquatic environments.  Field work requires travel for up to 100 days a year. 
Remainder of the year: Conduct advanced data analysis to interpret spatial distribution and movement patterns of aquatic animals, and contribute to scientific writing.
You will be expected to complete analyses and author or co-author peer-reviewed reports and manuscripts for publication in scientific journals — an excellent opportunity to build your publication record.

Desired Qualifications

Required:

Master's or Ph.D. in Aquatic Ecology, Animal Movement Ecology, Fishery Biology, Aquatic Biology, Biostatistics, or a closely related field
Experience with hazardous outdoor fieldwork conducted from a boat
Extensive experience navigating boats (up to 20 ft) in large water bodies with challenging conditions — current, wind, and tidal dynamics
Formal education/training in statistical methods used to describe animal spatial distribution, movement, and behavior
Expertise in fish telemetry technologies such as Innovasea and JSATS systems
Preferred:

Comfort operating fishing nets and working outdoors in all weather conditions, including hot, cold, wet, dry, windy, and icy environments
Experience as a lead author of scientific publications in peer reviewed journals. 
Location

This is a home-based position, but fieldwork will be conducted out of the Columbia River Research Station in Cook, WA. Applicants must live within approximately a 90-minute drive of this location and should expect to report to the Cook, WA lab throughout the 4–6 month field season.

Timing

Start date: No later than January 4, 2027

Appointment length: One to two years, depending on level of entry

Schedule: 40 hours per week, up to 1,928 hours per year

Salary and Benefits

Pay rate: $41.51–$49.74 per hour

Travel expenses will be paid by USGS

Please note that this is a Student Services Contractor (SSC) position, which differs from a standard employee appointment in the following ways:

SSCs are not eligible to participate in employee medical insurance or retirement plans

SSCs do not receive premium (overtime) pay for work beyond eight hours/day or 40 hours/week

SSCs are paid only for hours actually worked, with no holiday or annual leave benefits

 

Who Should Apply

This position is ideal for a motivated early-career scientist who is comfortable working independently in physically demanding field conditions and who also enjoys the analytical and writing side of research. If you're looking to build real-world experience in fish telemetry, spatial ecology, and scientific publishing, we encourage you to apply.

How to Apply

To apply send resume listing experience, education, publications, and graduation or expected graduation dates to Summer Burdick sburdick@usgs.gov. Applications will be accepted until September 25, 2026.

SUMMARY: 
 The Arkansas Game and Fish Commission (AGFC) Conservation Program Biologist II (FISHERIES DIVISION) is responsible for supervising a fisheries management resource.  This position is governed by state and federal laws and agency/institution policy.
 TYPICAL FUNCTIONS:
 Supervises a small to medium-sized professional staff by interviewing, recommending hire or termination, assigning and reviewing work, evaluating employee       performance, and training employees. 
Addresses program, district, hatchery, and divisional administrative duties
Directs the planning, preparation, and implementation of projects on Arkansas’ streams, rivers, reservoirs, and fish culture facilities.
Develops aquatic species conservation plans, aquatic species management plans, stream and river management plans, and reservoir management plans.  
Coordinates and leads biological surveys and studies of aquatic fauna, determining vital rate functions that shape population structure and condition. Statistically analyzes data, writes summary reports, and publishes peer-reviewed journal articles.
Coordinates the gathering of public input through public meetings, angler creel surveys, and other survey methods.
Communicates regularly with the appropriate assistant chief and/or fisheries district coordinators regarding oversight for budgets, contracts, and grants. 
 Develops and maintains program, district, or hatchery budgets. 
Serves on internal working groups, as well as external statewide, regional, and national working groups and teams.
Coordinates public relations work with various agencies, private industry, professional and civic organizations, and outdoor recreational groups. 
Must understand and be willing to function in a multi-faceted, team-oriented work environment. Must maintain close individual contact with and develop solid working relationships with all Fisheries Division, agency, and partner organization personnel.
Performs other duties as assigned.
 SPECIFIC JOB DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES:
 As an AGFC District Fisheries Supervisor (Conservation Program Biologist II), you will join a highly-trained, progressive team of fisheries scientists working to improve conservation and management of aquatic resources in Arkansas. 
 You will receive outstanding training and competitive pay and benefits, and are responsible for fisheries management activities within a district, with opportunities to collaborate on projects throughout the state. Job duties include: standardized fish population surveys, onsite and offsite angler surveys, stakeholder engagement, fish habitat improvement projects, analysis of survey data, preparation of annual fishery sample report management plans, all district administrative duties, fishing access development, and working with other agencies and elected officials on improving fisheries resources.
 This position serves as the Fisheries District 4 Supervisor in east central Arkansas, and other duties include:

·         Coordinating field sampling in a nine-county area 
·         Managing district budget and assets
·         Leading staff of full-time management biologist and part-time biological technician
·         Providing management assistance to owners of private waterbodies
·         Recommending changes to harvest regulations on public waterbodies
·         Drafting waterbody management plans
·         Leading district to meet the waterbody management plan, division, and agency strategic plan objectives
 KNOWLEDGE, ABILITIES, AND SKILLS:
 ·         Knowledge of the principles of biology, ecology, and related environmental sciences 
·         Knowledge of fisheries principles and techniques
·         Knowledge of laboratory and field survey equipment, techniques, and procedures 
·         Knowledge of supervisory practices and procedures 
·         Knowledge of state purchasing procedures 
·         Ability to plan work unit objectives and operational activities and to assign and direct the work of subordinates 
·         Ability to make public presentations
·         Ability to plan and direct scientific surveys and studies 
·         Ability to develop, implement, and monitor fisheries plans and programs

PRFERRED KNOWLEDGE, ABILITIES, AND SKILLS:
 ·         Knowledge of fish population dynamics, population simulation modeling, and common statistical analysis
·         Skill in working with the public
·         Experience in current fish sampling techniques
·         Good written and verbal communication skills
·         Physically able to work long hours, sometimes under harsh or physically demanding conditions
·         Strong teamwork concept, yet capable of completing a task without close supervision
·         Strong organizational skills. 
 MINIMUM EDUCATION AND/OR EXPERIENCE:  
 The formal education equivalent of a bachelor's degree in biology, ecology, fisheries management, or a related field; plus three years of experience in fisheries or a related field, including one year in a leadership capacity.
 OTHER JOB-RELATED EDUCATION AND/OR EXPERIENCE MAY BE SUBSTITUTED FOR ALL OR PART OF THESE BASIC REQUIREMENTS, EXCEPT FOR CERTIFICATION OR LICENSURE REQUIREMENTS, UPON APPROVAL OF THE HUMAN RESOURCES CHIEF.
 PREFERRED MINIMUM EDUCATION AND/OR EXPERIENCE:
 A  master's degree in fisheries management 
 SPECIAL JOB DIMENSIONS:
 Frequent in-state travel and field work with exposure to inclement weather are required.  
 CERTIFICATES, LICENSES, REGISTRATIONS:
 Must possess a valid Arkansas driver’s license.
Class A CDL may be required based on job duties assigned.
Must acquire and maintain professional accreditation in the area of expertise.
 ADDITIONAL INFORMATION: 
 The duty station for this position may be either the Brinkley Regional Office or the Joe Hogan State Fish Hatchery in Lonoke.
 For additional information, contact Justin Homan at 870-318-5987.
 All applicants are subject to a criminal background check.

Description
We are seeking 4 field technicians for muskrat monitoring and sampling operations in Illinois. This project aims to evaluate muskrat movement behavior, space use, survival, dispersal, and pathogen prevalence across contrasting landscapes to help inform restoration and management decisions. This project is being conducted through the Center for Wildlife Sustainability Research at Southern Illinois University in collaboration with the Illinois Department of Natural Resources. Technicians will work directly with SIU graduate students and research staff.

Selected candidates will carry out an intensive effort to conduct telemetry monitoring of collared muskrats as well as water and sediment sampling in west-central or southern Illinois. Toward the latter portion of the field season, technicians will potentially assist with muskrat necropsy.

We have 4 openings across 3 distinct timeframes for this posting: 

·      January – March 2027 
·      January – July 2027 
·      February – July 2027 

When applying, please clearly list all timeframes you are interested in and state if you are available for an early start (around December 28, 2026).

Pay rate begins at $16/hr, commensurate with experience, with a maximum of 37.5 hours/week. Work schedules will vary depending on weather, project priorities, and travel distance to field sites.

Housing will be provided.

Primary Responsibilities 

Conduct VHF telemetry tracking and mortality monitoring. 
Search on foot for muskrat signs (tracks, huts, scat, etc.). 
Collect water and sediment samples. 
Accurately collect and process data.
Operate 4WD university vehicles. 
Work safely in wetland environments under variable weather conditions. 
Assist with troubleshooting field logistics and equipment issues.

Ability to walk through wetlands, dense vegetation, mud, and uneven terrain. 
Ability to spend multiple hours in the car each day traveling to field sites.
Strong communication skills and attention to detail.

Preferred Qualifications 

Wildlife handling experience, particularly muskrat or small mammal trapping.
Experience with VHF telemetry, including homing and triangulation techniques.
Communication skills with landowners, the public, and agency staff

Hands on experience with chemical immobilization. 
Experience coordinating field logistics, gear, or equipment management.

Description
Email subject line for applications: “PJ-Project Manager” 
Applications will be accepted through the January 2027 with application review and interviews starting late November 2026. 
 About the project: Working with the Rocky Mountain Research Station (USFS), we are assessing experimental fuels reduction treatments in pinyon-juniper woodlands at sites in southwestern Utah. Between May and early October 2027, we will be conducting a 3-year and 1-year post treatment assessment at 1 and 2 field sites, respectively. Assessments will include tree survival and growth, tree seedling recruitment, understory herbaceous and woody shrub cover, and fuels evaluation. Additionally, we will be remeasuring stem maps and tree microsites to evaluate understory responses.
 About the position: The Project Manager (PM) will act as the liaison, or point of contact, between UNLV – the PI and senior research staff – and RMRS project lead(s) for a Pinyon-Juniper fuels reduction project and experiment in Southwest Utah. The PM will participate in project organization, scheduling, and coordination; field data collection, task assignment, and daily project management; and data and database management. The PM’s responsibilities will include coordinating schedules and tasks with the PI, UNLV senior research personnel, and RMRS staff; communicating schedules and delegating tasks to field crew members; ensuring adherence to a work plan and communicating scheduling adjustments to the PI, UNLV staff, and RMRS staff; submitting pre- and post-travel paperwork per University and the School of Life Science policy; providing post-trip updates, reports, and post-trip field itineraries, which will be submitted with quarterly fiscal reports to sponsor agency; ensuring protocol implementation and compliance; contributing to field data collection and field data management; maintaining field data and ensuring adherence to sampling protocols; working with the PI, UNLV, and RMRS staff to ensure data integrity (quality assurance/quality control); working with UNLV personnel to develop and maintain project databases and metadata, including for photograph, plant specimens, and sample archives; develop travel routes to navigate (driving, hiking) to field sites to ensure crew safety; communicating camping locations and hiking routes to UNLV contacts; and monitoring field safety conditions (weather, wildfire) in collaboration with UNLV research staff. 
 Please see our website for position expectations 

Preferred qualifications:
Master of Science in ecology, forestry, biology, resource management, environmental science, or field-biology-related discipline in which project management was demonstrably part of the degree experience
3+ years project and data management (professional or academic): team scheduling, communication and organization, fieldwork planning, driving and hiking navigation route planning, field data collection (electronic or paper datasheets), data and database management, equipment and supplies management, and protocol implementation and training. 
Working with mapping programs, such as ArcGIS Pro/ArcGIS Online or Google Earth; offline field data collection applications like Field Maps, and data management programs such as Microsoft Office Products, Google Workspace, and R.
3+ years of outdoor experience: field navigation, GPS, map/aerial imagery and compass navigation; 4WD on forest or desert unpaved roads, driving backcountry roads, route troubleshooting; hiking off trail cross country across uneven terrain; hiking and camping potentially in adverse weather conditions; hiking and camping in arid or semi-arid conditions.
1+ years of experience working with government agency personnel, including participation in communication of activities and planning; working directly or indirectly with government agencies
Experience conducting standard forest overstory and understory measurements; and plant identification experience using dichotomous keys, plant identification guides, or online resources; or experience conducting habitat assessments

Minimum requirements and qualifications for all field-based professional contract positions
Current U.S. State driver’s license; no at-fault accidents in the past five years; clean driving record; ability and willingness to drive
2+ years cumulative outdoor experience (on/off trail hiking, primitive/non-primitive camping, backpacking, field navigation with GPS/maps/compass, and 4WD driving and navigation)
1+ years 4-wheel drive experience 
Completed BA/BS in botany, microbiology, ecology, biology, environmental science, natural resources, or related fields
Minimum 1 year cumulative academic/professional experience in field-based research or plant community surveys, and plant identification using dichotomous keys
 1+ years computer experience (Microsoft Office, Open Office, Google Suite)
 
Physical capabilities and proficiency:
Walking 3 to 15 kilometers per day
Carrying to 15-35 lbs for long distances 
Lifting material up to 50 lbs
 Able to work 10-12 hours a day
Comfort working in semi-remote/remote locations
 
About our Lab: The Conservation Ecology Laboratory at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, led by Dr. Scott Abella, advances restoration ecology and applied conservation science through research that directly informs land management. Working closely with resource managers and scientific partners, we investigate the ecological factors that shape ecosystem recovery following human‑caused disturbances. Our team develops, tests, and evaluates restoration and mitigation strategies that vary in cost, resource requirements, and implementation effort, providing practical guidance for conservation and land‑management decision‑making.

The Conservation Ecology Laboratory is a grant-funded research laboratory with a mission of offering career-building opportunities focused on early to mid-career professional and applied skills development. While our positions are centered around ecology and applied research, most positions provide opportunities to develop transferable skills and abilities to other research- and science-based and non-science-based positions.
 
Contract details: This is a full‑time, temporary‑limited (no more than 24 months) Letter of Appointment (LOA) professional Research Assistant role with the University of Nevada Las Vegas - Nevada System of Higher Education (NSHE). The current position is for up to a 9 month appointment. LOA positions include healthcare benefits and require mandatory participation in the FICA Alternative Plan per university policy. Please consider reviewing these materials briefly before reaching out with general questions.
Benefits: https://www.unlv.edu/hr/benefits/loa
Retirement: https://www.unlv.edu/hr/benefits/retirement/fica and https://www.unlv.edu/hr/benefits/retirement/part-time

Meals per diem is project‑ and trip-dependent and administered according to university policies governing off‑campus travel. Meals per diem is offered during travel for this project (estimates based on Federal GSA M&IE rates) when departing and returning to UNLV. 
Meals per diem policy: https://www.unlv.edu/controller/travel-program/meal-diem

Before Applying: We suggest applicants review the position descriptions, minimum and preferred qualifications and requirements, benefits (healthcare, FICA), and seasonal or climate conditions for the work region(s) during the proposed contract period. If applicable, we strongly encourage applicants to research cost‑of‑living and consider a housing or living situation in advance of submitting an application. While we can recommend how to search for housing or regional camping locations, UNLV does not provide housing.

On-boarding Requirements: Applicants must be willing to communicate by email and phone 2–3 weeks before a negotiated contract start date to initiate the hiring process. If you are unable to have a communication with our administrative staff, the offer for employment will be rescinded.

All hires must report to the UNLV Maryland Campus on or before their first contract day and on a business day to complete in‑person I‑9 verification. Please review the I‑9 form in advance to ensure you qualify and have the required documentation. If you are unable to report to campus on the agreed start date or arrive without proper documentation, employment will be delayed and an offer can be rescinded.

To Apply: Email application materials (cover letter, resume/CV, 2-3 references) to lindsay.chiquoine@unlv.edu. Use the email subject line as specified for the position of interest. Emails without this subject line may be missed. We will do our best to acknowledge receipt of your application. Otherwise, if your application is selected, we will be in touch.
 
Please include:
A well-organized resume or curriculum vitae (CV) that includes your education, relevant coursework if applicable, job or experience history relevant to the position of interest, and per job, a list or short narrative on the aims, duties, and responsibilities using action words. Feel free to include a call-out section of relevant skills, abilities, and knowledge applicable to the position of interest. We request that resumes and CV's do not include photographs, images, or colored motifs to ensure your document is printable or transferable to grayscale. 
A cover letter indicating the position of interest, your availability, and relevant background and skills, abilities, and knowledge as they relate to the position. 
Clearly identify the position you are applying to in the first sentence, your availability dates (e.g., available during the posted position dates), whether your availability is flexible or if you have specific preferences for or hard start and end dates, and your relevant experience.
Clearly outline relevant experience, skills, abilities, and knowledge, and explain how your skills, abilities, and knowledge can be applied to the responsibilities and duties or project described. 
Translate past experiences into specific ways to contribute, rather than repeating or restating the resume or CV. 
Remain focused on job-related qualifications and avoid personal stories, informal anecdotes, or narrative elements not directly connected to the position. 
2–3 references: The individuals title (Dr., Mr. Ms.), name, position (professor, ecologist, botanist, biologist, field crew lead), where they work or worked, contact information, preferably email, and how you know them. 

Applications with be screened. Those that do not meet professional standards or do not address skills, abilities, and knowledge may not be forwarded for further consideration. Anonymized applications may be shared with PIs and project partners for specific programs.

Background:
Established in 1961, the Ruffed Grouse Society (RGS) is North America’s foremost conservation organization dedicated to creating healthy forests, abundant wildlife, and promoting a conservation ethic. Together with the American Woodcock Society (AWS), established in 2014, RGS & AWS work with private landowners and government agencies to develop critical wildlife habitat utilizing scientific management practices.

RGS & AWS has entered into a collaborative agreement with the Natural Resources Conservation Services (NRCS). Together, RGS & AWS and NRCS are looking for a motivated individual to work effectively with private landowners and other stakeholders in the north-central region of Wisconsin. The Forest Wildlife Specialist will function as a Wildlife Forester, providing conservation technical assistance.

Qualifications:
•A degree in forestry and/or closely related field, with 2+ years of experience and/or a graduate degree in natural resource management.
•Knowledge of forest ecology, forest management, forest operations, silviculture and farming related to land management in the northern forest region of Wisconsin. Ability to assess wildlife habitat and connect forest management and habitat needs.
•Excellent spoken and written communication skills, networking skills, organization, and ability to engage with diverse collaborators. Must be comfortable speaking in public and engaging landowners on a one-to-one basis.
•Ability to use MS Word, Excel, ArcGIS, Field Maps and other computer mapping systems to identify and delineate project boundaries.
•Willingness and ability to frequently travel throughout north-central Wisconsin and perform arduous fieldwork in difficult terrain and various weather conditions.
•Applicant must be self-motivated and responsible. Required ability to work independently and manage multiple projects under deadlines. Ability to produce effective results and problem-solve.
•The position must participate in specific training programs to use partner facilities and equipment. Applicant must have a valid driver’s license.

Position Summary:
Work jointly with the RGS & AWS and the NRCS to increase forest diversity and enhance habitat for
forest wildlife by working with landowners to implement the Federal Farm Bill and other wildlife
conservation programs. The successful candidate will provide technical assistance to landowners to
develop forest management plans and implement forest management practices via the Environmental
Quality Incentives Program (EQIP), Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP) and other federal, state
and local programs.

Duties will also include writing forest management plans, contract development and coordination, site
assessment and monitoring, accomplishment reporting and development and implementation of outreach
and educational efforts that will lead to broader adoption of active forest management by private
landowners and public agencies. Coordinate outreach and wildlife habitat management efforts with RGS
& AWS, NRCS, WDNR and other partner staff, especially related to the restoration and enhancement of
young forest habitats.

Attendance at relevant RGS & AWS, NRCS and WDNR meetings will also be required. Assisting with
regional forest conservation projects on public and private lands and attending RGS & AWS
member/fundraising events may be required.

Compensation:
Competitive compensation; health insurance including medical, dental and vision; retirement options
including employer contribution; a government vehicle for most business travel; a purchasing card for
business and travel expenses; computer and printer; cell phone; office supplies and continuing education
training and support as needed to excel will be provided. Salary commensurate with experience,
minimum starting $50,000–$59,900.

Application Instructions:
Please email a cover letter and resume combined in a single .pdf file by October 18th, 2026, to
JaredE@RuffedGrouseSociety.org using "WI Forest Wildlife Specialist" as the email subject line.
Submission of 3 references as part of the application submission is required.

Questions regarding this position can be directed to Jared Elm at (715)-450-2531 or JaredE@RuffedGrouseSociety.org

Email subject line for Botanist applicants: "2027 Winter-Spring Botanist"
Salary $4,300 - $4,500/mo., DOE 
Preferred start date: 02/01/2027
Interviews are scheduled for mid-October through mid-November, with initial offers sent by late November. 

This position is ideal for a mid-career professional seeking to strengthen field project management skills, plant identification using botany skills (e.g., using dichotomous keys and taxonomic resources), field navigation abilities, leadership and communication abilities, research experience, data management abilities, and field-to-lab integration skills. Applicants with regional botany knowledge, botanical expertise, and/or outdoor work experience specifically within the Mojave Desert Ecoregion are strongly preferred. 
 This position is 95% field‑based, requiring comfort working outdoors for extended periods in semi-remote-to-remote desert environments. All applicants must demonstrate 2 years cumulative outdoor experience including participation in professional or academic data collection, camping, hiking, or backpacking to demonstrate outdoor capabilities and tolerances. Most of the field season will follow a hitch-based schedule (8-days on/6-days off) and will require camping near field sites, as well as some technical four-wheel driving to access field sites. An anticipated schedule is posted on our website and will be updated as we finalize project tasks and itineraries. 
 Duties/responsibilities: A 2 to 4-person crew will drive and hike to monitoring plots in southeastern California and southern Nevada, conduct site assessments and plant community surveys following protocols, identify detected species, manage field data, and back up data at the University of Nevada Las Vegas. The botanist additionally will be responsible for daily field project management and scheduling tasks, coordinating with research staff and the PI, accurately identifying and documenting detected species, maintaining a species list, and documenting resources used for plant identification. 
  Preferred qualifications for botanist: 
·         Master of Science in botany, ecology, natural resources, or related degree, or equivalent professional experience 
·         3+ years (academic/professional) botany/plant-focused surveys using dichotomous keys, plant identification guides, and online resources; maintaining a species list, documenting species using notes and photographs, and documenting resources are used for plant identification (please highlight in a resume or cover letter botany location experience and plant identification resources used). 
·         Experience with southeastern California and southern Nevada Mojave Desert flora and related keys/plant identification resources 
·         2+ years contributing to project and data management: following quality assurance and quality control standards for field data, recording and updating metadata, and contributing to hard-copy data and database management and maintenance 
·         Science laboratory experience (academic or professional), following laboratory protocols, managing samples and data, participating in sample inventory and database management 

Minimum requirements and qualifications for all field-based professional contract positions 
·         Current U.S. State driver’s license; no at-fault accidents in the past five years; clean driving record; ability and willingness to drive 
·         2+ years cumulative outdoor experience (on/off trail hiking, primitive/non-primitive camping, backpacking, field navigation with GPS/maps/compass, and 4WD driving and navigation) 
·         1+ years 4-wheel drive experience 
·         Completed BA/BS in botany, microbiology, ecology, biology, environmental science, natural resources, or related fields 
·         Minimum 1 year cumulative academic/professional experience in field-based research or plant community surveys, and plant identification using dichotomous keys 
·         1+ years computer experience (Microsoft Office, Open Office, Google Suite) 

Physical capabilities and proficiency: 
·         Walking 3 to 15 kilometers per day 
·         Carrying to 15-35 lbs for long distances 
·         Lifting material up to 50 lbs 
·         Able to work 10-12 hours a day 
·         Comfort working in semi-remote/remote locations 

About our Lab: The Conservation Ecology Laboratory at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, led by Dr. Scott Abella, advances restoration ecology and applied conservation science through research that directly informs land management. Working closely with resource managers and scientific partners, we investigate the ecological factors that shape ecosystem recovery following human‑caused disturbances. Our team develops, tests, and evaluates restoration and mitigation strategies that vary in cost, resource requirements, and implementation effort, providing practical guidance for conservation and land‑management decision‑making. 
 The Conservation Ecology Laboratory is a grant-funded research laboratory with a mission of offering career-building opportunities focused on early to mid-career professional and applied skills development. While our positions are centered around ecology and applied research, most positions provide opportunities to develop transferable skills and abilities to other research- and science-based and non-science-based positions. 
 Contract details: This is a full‑time, temporary‑limited (no more than 24 months) Letter of Appointment (LOA) professional Research Assistant role with the University of Nevada Las Vegas - Nevada System of Higher Education (NSHE). LOA positions include healthcare benefits and require mandatory participation in the FICA Alternative Plan per university policy. Please consider reviewing these materials briefly before reaching out with general questions. 
 Benefits: https://www.unlv.edu/hr/benefits/loa 
Retirement: https://www.unlv.edu/hr/benefits/retirement/fica and https://www.unlv.edu/hr/benefits/retirement/part-time 
 Before Applying: We suggest potential applicants review the position descriptions, minimum and preferred qualifications and requirements, benefits (healthcare, FICA), and seasonal or climate conditions for the work region(s) during the proposed contract period. If applicable, we strongly encourage potential applicants to research cost‑of‑living and consider a housing or living situation in advance of submitting an application. While we can recommend how to search for housing or regional camping locations, UNLV does not provide housing. Most of our students commute to campus and live in the surrounding community or across the valley. 
 On-boarding Requirements: Applicants must be willing to communicate by email and phone 2–3 weeks before a negotiated contract start date to initiate the hiring process. If you are unable to have a communication with our administrative staff, the offer for employment will be rescinded. 
 All hires must report to the UNLV Maryland Campus on or before their first contract day and on a business day to complete in‑person I‑9 verification. Please review the I‑9 form in advance to ensure you qualify and have the required documentation. If you are unable to report to campus on the agreed start date or arrive without proper documentation, employment will be delayed and an offer can be rescinded. 

All new employees will be required to participate in on-boarding training, including Cybersecurity Awareness and Preventing Harassment and Discrimination. Training is required to be completed before the end of the first week on contract. We will let you know if Chemical Hygiene or Defensive Driving training is required for your position.  
 To Apply: Email application materials (cover letter, resume/CV, 2-3 references) to lindsay.chiquoine@unlv.edu. Use the email subject line as specified for the position of interest. Emails without this subject line may be missed. We will do our best to acknowledge receipt of your application. Otherwise, if your application is selected, we will be in touch. 
Please include: 
A well-organized resume or curriculum vitae (CV) that includes your education, relevant coursework if applicable, job or experience history relevant to the position of interest, and per job, a list or short narrative on the aims, duties, and responsibilities using action words. Feel free to include a call-out section of relevant skills, abilities, and knowledge applicable to the position of interest. We request that resumes and CV's do not include photographs, images, or colored motifs to ensure your document is printable or transferable to grayscale. If these items are present, they will be removed before review. 
A cover letter indicating the position of interest, your availability, and relevant background and skills, abilities, and knowledge as they relate to the position. 
Clearly identify the position you are applying to in the first sentence, your availability dates (e.g., available during the posted position dates), whether your availability is flexible or if you have specific preferences for or hard start and end dates, and your relevant experience.
Clearly outline relevant experience, skills, abilities, and knowledge, and explain how your skills, abilities, and knowledge can be applied to the responsibilities and duties or project described. 
Translate past experiences into specific ways to contribute, rather than repeating or restating the resume or CV. 
Remain focused on job-related qualifications and avoid personal stories, informal anecdotes, or narrative elements not directly connected to the position. These will be deleted or blacked out before review. 
2–3 references: The individuals title (Dr., Mr. Ms.), name, position (professor, ecologist, botanist, biologist, field crew lead), where they work or worked, contact information, preferably email, and how you know them. 

Applications with be screened. Those that do not meet professional standards or do not address skills, abilities, and knowledge may not be forwarded for further consideration. Anonymized applications may be shared with PIs and project partners for specific programs.

Lindsay Chiquoine

Are you a self motivated, hard-working individual? Then the Pigeon Key Foundation, a 501(c) not-for-profit organization, is looking for you to be a part of our 2027 intern team. Start date January 18th with a TBD end date in mid-August. Possibility of full-time employment may exist to hired interns who demonstrate a superior ability at the position. Internship provides weekly stipend and on-island housing, as well as food when groups are present. Marine Science Education Intern Responsibilities: **This list is not exhaustive but will give interested applicants a better idea of what jobs will be required of them. We are a small organization. If you do not agree with the statement “if a task needs doing, it is in my job description” please do not apply for this internship. ** • Marine Education (55% of internship) o Lead both classroom and hands-on learning activities for students age K-college on a variety of marine science subjects. Hands-on activities include fishing, kayaking, snorkeling, and invertebrate collection. o Days will be long (sometimes 6am-10pm) and often include weekends. Other group-related tasks will include cooking, cleaning, equipment prep/clean-up, etc. o While groups are on-island they are our number one priority. o Summer Camps (6-7 weeks in June/July/August) will require interns to perform all of the above duties, plus participate in camp activities and be overnight counselors in the student dorms • Island Maintenance (25% of internship) o When groups are not on island, interns will be responsible for island upkeep and preparing for upcoming groups. o Days will be mostly 9am-5pm M-F schedule, but that can change based on what needs doing and the weather. o Will include, but not limited to, cleaning, sweeping, mopping, raking, weed whacking, washing sheets, painting, maintaining island grounds, cleaning aquariums, etc. • Office Work (5%) o Making group workbooks, expanding and updating curriculum, maintaining membership list, writing articles for the foundation's newsletter, blog entries, etc. o Interns with demonstrated responsibility and integrity may be asked to assist with the foundation’s social media accounts (facebook, instagram, etc.) • Various (15%) o Representing the foundation at various events in the community, running work errands, outreach programs, summer camps, etc. This list is not exhaustive. The successful applicant will be able to live and work well with people of various backgrounds in a small-work environment. The ability to separate personal issues from professional time (and the ability to resolve any personal issues quickly with little conflict) is crucial to this position. Interns will live on Pigeon Key, a 5-acre island in the middle of the Florida Keys and a historical landmark. Interns are encouraged to dive, fish, and explore the Florida Keys island chain on their days off, which are limited but do exist! Qualifications: - Recent graduate of a degree program in biology, marine biology, zoology, science education, or a related field. - A high level of interest (experience preferred) in teaching students of diverse ages and backgrounds - Excellent public speaking skills for audiences of various ages and abilities - Experienced swimmer (preference will be given to applicants with current or previous lifeguarding, instructing, or diving experience) - An optimistic, “can-do” attitude - Willingness to cook, clean, and do yardwork - The ability to work independently and in a team setting while foreseeing and quickly correcting potential problems - The ability to work well with others in a small organization where your coworkers are also your roommates. -Experience with Microsoft Office, Google Drive and various social media formats preferred but not required.

Fisheries management

Fence building and repair

Facilities maintenance and repair
Landscaping and grounds upkeep
